title: Vertex LegalTech - audit log latency escalation (delivery lag + interim mitigation)
summary: Vertex escalated that audit logs in their Redwood Private/VPC deployment are arriving 30–45 minutes late, causing gaps in their compliance monitoring and alerting. Redwood confirmed the audit-log pipeline can backlog under specific load patterns and that there is currently no customer-visible lag metric/alert. The team aligned on expectations (targeting single-digit minutes, with defined thresholds by tier), immediate mitigations (widen export window, implement retries/backoff, avoid treating the feed as real-time until fixed), and an engineering plan tied to SUP-1846 / ENG-4824 to add a first-class lag metric + alerting + runbook updates. Rachel owned customer comms cadence and a written mitigation note; SRE owned confirming current backlog status and a timeline for the alert rollout.
topics: SUP-1846 context and current customer impact
Audit log delivery expectations vs current behavior
Interim mitigations (export window, retries, operational guardrails)
Engineering plan: lag metric, dashboard, alert thresholds (ENG-4824)
Customer comms cadence + what will be on status vs direct email
next_steps: Redwood (Sean) to confirm root cause hypothesis + current backlog status from dashboards and share customer-safe summary by EOD
Redwood (Allison) to share proposed lag thresholds (warn/critical) aligned to enterprise expectations and SLO policy
Redwood (Ethan) to post ENG-4824 implementation timeline and confirm whether a temporary manual monitor can be set up this week
Redwood (Rachel) to send Vertex a written interim mitigation guide (retry policy + export window guidance) and update cadence
Vertex (Mark/Priya) to confirm their SIEM polling/ingestion assumptions (near-real-time vs batch) and whether they can tolerate a temporary 15–30 min window
action_items: Sean Gallagher - Pull last 72h audit log pipeline lag data for Vertex tenant and confirm whether backlog correlates with regional batch jobs - 2026-02-10
Allison Grant - Draft customer-facing SLO language proposal for audit log delivery (p95 target + max acceptable delay) for enterprise tiers - 2026-02-12
Ethan Park - Update ENG-4824 with implementation steps (metric, alert, runbook link, customer-visible dashboard) and share ETA - 2026-02-11
Dev Patel - Add interim mitigation steps to KB draft and cross-link from SUP-1846 internal notes - 2026-02-11
Rachel Kim - Send customer comms email with agreed mitigations + timeline; include what is and isn’t promised - 2026-02-10
transcript:
Meeting: Vertex LegalTech - audit log latency escalation (delivery lag + interim mitigation)
Recorded: 2026-02-10 16:00 UTC
Duration: 41 min
Attendees (Redwood): Rachel Kim, Dev Patel, Sean Gallagher, Allison Grant, Ethan Park
Attendees (Vertex): Priya Desai (Security Eng), Mark Ellison (Platform Eng), Lena Wu (Compliance Ops)

[00:00] Rachel Kim: Alright, let’s get started. Thanks everyone for jumping on short notice. This is the audit log latency escalation. I want to make sure we’re aligned on (1) what you’re seeing, (2) what we think is happening, (3) what you can do right now to reduce impact, and (4) the timeline for the metric and alerting improvements we have in flight.

[00:20] Priya Desai: Yep, thank you. This has been pretty disruptive on our side. We have compliance monitoring that expects… not necessarily instant, but not forty minutes later.

[00:31] Mark Ellison: Yeah, the delay basically breaks correlation for incident response. We’ve got CloudTrail and other sources coming in close-ish to real time, then Redwood shows up half an hour later.

[00:44] Rachel Kim: Understood. Sean and Allison are here from SRE/observability, Ethan from Platform. Dev is from Support Ops, he’s tracking the ticket. Dev, do you want to anchor us in the case details so we all use the same facts?

[00:56] Dev Patel: Sure. This is SUP-1846. Vertex reported audit log delivery lag over 30 minutes—peaking around 45 minutes—starting late last week and continuing intermittently. Affected environment is their Private/VPC deployment. They’re consuming audit logs via the delivery pipeline into their SIEM; they’re noticing the timestamps in the payload are correct, but the arrival time is delayed.

[01:18] Lena Wu: Right, and our auditors care about “timely detection.” We can argue “eventually consistent,” but we need a documented expectation and we need alerting when it’s not meeting it.

[01:31] Rachel Kim: Makes sense. Priya, can you quickly say what your internal expectation is? Like, what would you consider acceptable, and where does it become a compliance risk?

[01:41] Priya Desai: We can tolerate single-digit minutes. Under 10 is fine. Fifteen starts to get uncomfortable. Over 30 means our analysts are looking at the wrong picture.

[01:52] Mark Ellison: And to be clear, we’re not asking for “hard real time,” but we need a stated SLO for delivery and a mechanism to monitor it.

[02:02] Sean Gallagher: Yep. That’s fair. I can share what we believe is going on. First, we do see periods where the audit pipeline backlogs. The system is designed to be durable—so it queues and drains rather than dropping logs—but the downside is you can get delivery lag.

[02:18] Sean Gallagher: What we don’t have today—and this is the gap—is a first-class “lag metric” that’s exposed and alerting aligned to enterprise expectations. That’s exactly what ENG-4824 is intended to address.

[02:34] Allison Grant: And just to add, we have internal telemetry, but it’s not packaged in a way Support or customers can easily interpret. So you end up asking us “is it behind” and we do a bunch of manual checks.

[02:47] Priya Desai: Okay, but why is it happening now? Did something change? Like a deploy or capacity issue?

[02:54] Ethan Park: We’re still narrowing it down. There were some internal changes to the batching behavior—this is not customer-visible in release notes because it’s an internal pipeline component. But it might have shifted burst patterns.

[03:08] Ethan Park: Also, on Private/VPC setups we sometimes see network egress constraints or downstream receiver throttling. I’m not saying that’s you, just listing the typical causes.

[03:19] Mark Ellison: Our receiver side hasn’t changed. Same ingestion pipeline. We can show you our throughput and it’s stable.

[03:26] Sean Gallagher: That’s helpful. If your receiver is stable, then it points more to Redwood-side backlog. I’ll confirm with the actual lag graphs after this call. I don’t want to hand-wave.

[03:39] Rachel Kim: Appreciate that. Let’s separate two tracks: immediate mitigation so your team can operate this week, and the product improvements for next.

[03:48] Rachel Kim: Allison, can you talk about what “expected” is supposed to be today? Because I think part of the escalation is: there wasn’t a clear expectation set.

[03:58] Allison Grant: Right. Today the documentation basically implies “near real time,” but it’s not quantified. Internally we’ve treated it as best-effort with the pipeline typically delivering within a few minutes. But “typically” is not an SLO.

[04:13] Allison Grant: What we’re proposing—subject to SRE and product sign-off—is an explicit delivery SLO like p95 under 5–10 minutes for enterprise tiers, and then define warning thresholds, like if lag exceeds 10 minutes for more than N minutes, and critical if it exceeds 30.

[04:33] Priya Desai: That would address the governance issue. We need to tell auditors “p95 under X.”

[04:39] Mark Ellison: But we also need to know when you violate it. A metric and an alert.

[04:44] Ethan Park: Agreed. ENG-4824 is: add a metric that measures end-to-end lag, add alerting, add a dashboard, and update the runbook. The implementation is being done in our observability pack as well as the pipeline service.

[04:58] Dev Patel: And to connect it: SUP-1846 is the support ticket and ENG-4824 is the engineering workstream.

[05:05] Rachel Kim: Great. Now—interim mitigations. Sean, what do we recommend customers do when audit logs are delayed? I know this is tricky because it depends on their ingestion.

[05:16] Sean Gallagher: Right. There are a few pragmatic mitigations:
- First: treat the stream as “eventually delivered,” not “real time.” Operationally, that means your SIEM correlation windows should include a larger lookback—like 60–90 minutes—so delayed events still trigger.
- Second: if you are pulling in batches, widen the export window and avoid frequent small polls that can amplify pressure.
- Third: implement retries with exponential backoff on the ingestion call, and make sure you are not dropping on transient 429 or timeouts.

[05:52] Priya Desai: We can widen correlation windows, but that creates noise. It’s not ideal.

[05:58] Mark Ellison: Also we’re not pulling, we’re receiving. But we can adjust how we process. We can delay alert evaluation for Redwood events until we believe the stream has caught up.

[06:10] Ethan Park: That’s a reasonable pattern: “hold back” evaluation by some offset. Like you assume Redwood logs might arrive 30 minutes late, then treat the event time accordingly. Not pretty, but safe.

[06:22] Lena Wu: Can you provide a written statement that this is temporary and you’re implementing alerting? For audit and for our internal risk register.

[06:32] Rachel Kim: Yes. I’ll send an email after this with what we can commit to, plus the interim guidance. I’ll keep it customer-safe.

[06:42] Priya Desai: What do you mean by customer-safe? We need to know if you found root cause.

[06:48] Sean Gallagher: We can share a summary without internal system names. Like: “audit log delivery experienced backlog due to pipeline queueing under load; logs are durable, not dropped; we are implementing monitoring and alerting and working on reducing backlog.” That kind of language.

[07:07] Mark Ellison: Okay.

[07:09] Rachel Kim: Let’s talk timeline. Ethan, what’s realistic for ENG-4824?

[07:14] Ethan Park: The first step—metric definition and instrumenting the pipeline—can land this week. Dashboard and alerting is probably next week depending on review. I don’t want to overpromise, but the goal is within two weeks for “customer-visible” or at least support-visible lag monitoring.

[07:35] Allison Grant: We can do an internal dashboard sooner, like in 2–3 days, then wire the alert thresholds after we validate signal quality. It’s easy to create a noisy alert if you don’t baseline.

[07:48] Priya Desai: I’d accept internal for now if you can tell us “we see lag is 32 minutes” and “it’s trending down.” But longer term we need the alerting.

[07:58] Rachel Kim: Understood.

[08:00] Mark Ellison: Is this going to show up in your status page?

[08:04] Rachel Kim: For audit log lag, we generally do direct comms to impacted enterprise accounts unless it’s a broad multi-customer incident. If it becomes widespread, then we can evaluate a status update. Our comms policy is to avoid publishing customer-specific pipeline details publicly.

[08:23] Mark Ellison: Okay, but this feels pretty major to us.

[08:26] Rachel Kim: I hear you. We’ll keep you updated on a cadence we agree on—like daily until stable, then weekly until alerting is live.

[08:36] Priya Desai: Daily updates are fine for now.

[08:39] Sean Gallagher: To be concrete, I can send a brief note after I check the dashboards today: current lag, peak lag over last 24 hours, and whether backlog is draining.

[08:51] Dev Patel: And Support will mirror that in the ticket notes so we have a record.

[08:56] Rachel Kim: Great.

[09:00] Lena Wu: One more: are logs ever lost? Because our team is assuming we can reconcile later.

[09:06] Sean Gallagher: The design is at-least-once delivery. So “lost” is not expected, but duplicates are possible in edge cases. If you’re deduping on event ID, you’ll be safe.

[09:19] Mark Ellison: We do dedupe. We’ve seen duplicates rarely.

[09:23] Ethan Park: That matches at-least-once semantics.

[09:26] Priya Desai: Is there a documented semantics statement? Like exactly-once vs at-least-once?

[09:33] Rachel Kim: We can add that to the knowledge base article we’re publishing this sprint. Dev, that’s in scope, right?

[09:41] Dev Patel: Yes. We have a draft workaround article specifically for audit log delivery latency. It includes what to expect and temporary mitigations. We’ll add the delivery semantics line, and the “when to escalate” criteria.

[09:55] Priya Desai: Please also add “what evidence to gather” because when we open tickets, you always ask for IDs. For logs it’s not obvious.

[10:03] Dev Patel: Yep—timestamp ranges, example event IDs, and your ingestion timestamps. And region/deployment details.

[10:12] Rachel Kim: Good. Let’s dig into the technical details for a few minutes so Sean/Ethan can diagnose.

[10:18] Sean Gallagher: Mark, can you confirm: are you receiving logs via the HTTPS push endpoint or are you using the batch export API?

[10:24] Mark Ellison: We’re using the push to our collector endpoint. We terminate TLS at a load balancer, then forward to our ingestion.

[10:33] Sean Gallagher: Any 4xx or 5xx spikes on your endpoint when Redwood pushes?

[10:38] Mark Ellison: No. We looked. It’s stable. We can share metrics screenshots. We also didn’t see request floods, just… the requests arrive late.

[10:48] Allison Grant: That suggests backlog before egress. If there was downstream throttling, you’d see retries and error spikes.

[10:56] Ethan Park: Agreed.

[10:59] Priya Desai: Can you explain what “backlog” means here? Like messages queued in your system?

[11:06] Sean Gallagher: Yes—there’s an internal queue between event generation and delivery. If the downstream worker can’t drain at the same rate, lag grows. The reason can be throughput constraints, resource contention, or occasionally a “hot shard” effect.

[11:25] Mark Ellison: Is this per-tenant? Could another tenant impact us?

[11:30] Ethan Park: For Private/VPC, the control plane is logically isolated, but there are shared components depending on your configuration. I’ll be careful: your data is isolated, but infrastructure could still share some workers. We can validate whether your audit pipeline is dedicated or pooled.

[11:49] Priya Desai: We assumed “private” means fully isolated.

[11:53] Rachel Kim: For your contract, the data plane is isolated. Some control plane services can be shared unless specified. But let’s not litigate it live—Ethan can confirm the architecture for your deployment and we can follow up in writing.

[12:09] Lena Wu: Please do, because it matters for our risk review.

[12:13] Ethan Park: Understood.

[12:15] Sean Gallagher: Another question: are you seeing lag correlated with any batch jobs on your side? Like nightly compliance exports?

[12:22] Mark Ellison: Not that we can tell. It’s kind of random. Though maybe it’s worse during US morning.

[12:29] Allison Grant: That could align with platform load.

[12:32] Rachel Kim: Okay. Let’s move to commitments and comms.

[12:36] Rachel Kim: From our side: we’ll treat this as an enterprise-impacting issue. You’ll get daily updates until stable. Sean will send a technical status today. We’ll provide interim mitigation guidance. And we’ll deliver a metric and alerting improvements on the ENG-4824 timeline.

[12:56] Priya Desai: Can you give us an ETA for “alerting”? Like a date.

[13:01] Ethan Park: Tentatively: metric + internal dashboard by end of this week (Feb 13). Alerting tied to that metric by end of next week (Feb 20). That’s my best current estimate assuming no surprises.

[13:16] Sean Gallagher: And I’ll caveat: alert thresholds may be adjusted after we see baseline. But you’ll at least have visibility.

[13:26] Mark Ellison: Okay.

[13:28] Lena Wu: And does that include a runbook? Because we need to know what to do when it’s violated.

[13:33] Allison Grant: Yes, runbook updates are part of it. So Support and SRE will have an explicit “if lag > X then do Y” and a customer-facing escalation guidance.

[13:45] Dev Patel: We’ll include “when to escalate” in the KB article too, like: if lag > 15 minutes for more than 30 minutes, or if any single event is delayed > 30 minutes, open a P1 ticket for enterprise.

[14:01] Priya Desai: That’s good.

[14:03] Mark Ellison: One thing: we’re also concerned about retention. If there’s a backlog, do events expire?

[14:10] Sean Gallagher: Not in the queue for the timeframes we’re discussing. It’s not like a 5-minute TTL. But I’ll double-check the queue retention settings for your deployment.

[14:23] Ethan Park: Yeah, there are safeguards.

[14:25] Rachel Kim: Great.

[14:27] Priya Desai: Are there any knobs we can tune on our side? Like reduce volume? We have a lot of audit events.

[14:35] Ethan Park: Potentially. Some customers choose to filter high-volume low-value events, like repeated “token issued” events—depends what your audit requirements are. We can review event categories. But we need to be careful—some events might be required.

[14:52] Lena Wu: We probably can’t filter much.

[14:54] Mark Ellison: But we can batch in our pipeline. If we’re doing expensive parsing, we can do it later.

[15:00] Sean Gallagher: That helps your side, but doesn’t reduce Redwood backlog. Still worth doing to reduce pressure on your ingest endpoint.

[15:09] Rachel Kim: Let’s capture that as “customer-side mitigation”: widen windows, treat as delayed, avoid strict real-time assumptions.

[15:17] Priya Desai: Okay.

[15:19] Rachel Kim: I’m going to pause and ask: is there anything else you need from us today to de-escalate? Or is the plan acceptable pending the written follow-up?

[15:29] Priya Desai: The plan is acceptable. The key is the written statement and the timeline. And we want to make sure this doesn’t get deprioritized.

[15:39] Rachel Kim: Understood. This is tracked as an engineering task, not just a support note. We’ll keep it moving.

[15:46] Mark Ellison: Also, if it’s exceeding 30 minutes again, do we page someone? Or is it ticket-only?

[15:53] Sean Gallagher: For now: open or update the support ticket and reference “audit log lag > 30m.” Support can page SRE based on the escalation rubric. Once alerting is in place, SRE will be paged automatically when it crosses the critical threshold.

[16:11] Dev Patel: And we’ll make sure the escalation path is documented. We’re updating the playbook so the triggers are consistent.

[16:19] Lena Wu: Good.

[16:21] Rachel Kim: Cool. Let’s do a quick recap of next steps, then I’ll let you go.

[16:27] Rachel Kim: Sean: you’ll pull last 72 hours of lag and send a customer-safe summary today.

[16:33] Sean Gallagher: Correct.

[16:34] Rachel Kim: Allison: propose thresholds and SLO language.

[16:38] Allison Grant: Yep, I’ll draft and share internally first, then we can send externally.

[16:42] Rachel Kim: Ethan: update ENG-4824 timeline and confirm architecture isolation details for Vertex’s deployment.

[16:49] Ethan Park: Yes.

[16:50] Rachel Kim: Dev: update the KB draft with semantics, evidence to gather, and escalation guidance.

[16:56] Dev Patel: Will do.

[16:58] Rachel Kim: And I’ll send the customer email with interim mitigations and cadence, and we’ll do daily updates until stable.

[17:07] Priya Desai: Sounds good.

[17:09] Mark Ellison: Thanks everyone.

[17:11] Lena Wu: Thank you.

[17:13] Rachel Kim: Thanks. We’ll follow up shortly.

---
